title: Compilers, Interpreters and Virtual Machines
summary: A compiler translates a whole program into machine code before it runs; an interpreter reads the program and carries it out as it goes. Many languages do both - Java and C# compile to bytecode for a virtual machine, Python compiles to bytecode for its interpreter, and JavaScript engines compile the hot parts while running.
markdown:
## Two ways to run a language The CPU only runs machine code (4.05). So a program in any other language has to become machine code somehow. There are two basic strategies. ### Compile first A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code **ahead of time**. You get an executable file that runs directly on the CPU, with no translator needed any more. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["Source code
main.c"] -->|compiler| O["Machine code
(object file)"] -->|linker| E["Executable
program"] -->|run| CPU ``` C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift and Fortran work this way. The compilation itself takes a moment, but the result runs as fast as the hardware allows. The **linker** joins your code with code from libraries (such as the code behind `printf`) into one program. ### Interpret An **interpreter** is a program that reads your program and carries it out, step by step, **while it runs**. There is no separate machine-code file: the interpreter, which is itself a compiled program, does what each line says. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["Source code
main.py"] --> I["Interpreter
(a running program)"] --> R["The program's effects"] ``` Early BASIC was interpreted, and so are shell scripts. You can start instantly and change code without rebuilding, but every step costs extra work, so it is usually much slower. ## The trade-off | | Compiled | Interpreted | |---|---|---| | Speed of running | Fast: machine code | Slower: an interpreter does the work | | Start after a change | Build first | Immediately | | Errors in the code found | Many before it runs | Often only when that line runs | | Runs on | The CPU family it was built for | Anywhere the interpreter runs | ## The middle way: bytecode and virtual machines Most popular languages today do a bit of both. **Bytecode** is a compact, made-up instruction set for an imaginary computer - a **virtual machine** (VM). The language is compiled to bytecode once; then a program on the real computer runs the bytecode. | Language | Compiles to | Which is run by | |---|---|---| | **Java** (1995) | Java bytecode (`.class` files) | The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) | | **C#** (2000) | .NET intermediate language | The .NET runtime | | **Python** (1991) | Python bytecode (`.pyc` files, done automatically) | The Python interpreter's bytecode loop | | **WebAssembly** (2017) | Wasm bytecode | Every web browser | The bytecode is the same on every computer, so one compiled Java program runs on Windows, macOS and Linux: "write once, run anywhere". The VM is what differs per machine. You can see Python's bytecode yourself: ```python import dis def add(a, b): return a + b dis.dis(add) ``` `LOAD_FAST`, `BINARY_OP`, `RETURN_VALUE`: a tiny instruction set, very like the tiny computer of 4.04, which Python's interpreter fetches, decodes and executes in a loop. ## Just-in-time compilation A **JIT** (just-in-time) compiler watches a program while it runs, finds the parts that run most often - the **hot** loops - and compiles those to real machine code on the spot. The JVM, .NET and every JavaScript engine (Chrome's V8, Firefox's SpiderMonkey) do this, which is why Java, C# and JavaScript can be nearly as fast as compiled C for long-running programs. ```mermaid flowchart LR JS["JavaScript source"] --> P["Parse to bytecode"] --> I["Interpret it,
counting what runs often"] --> H{"Hot?"} H -->|yes| J["JIT: compile to
machine code"] --> CPU H -->|no| I ``` ## How this site runs your code Xenon uses all of these. C, C++, Rust and assembly are compiled (on Compiler Explorer, or on your computer in the desktop app) and the machine code is run. Java and C# are compiled to bytecode and run by their VMs. Python runs in its interpreter. JavaScript and TypeScript run in your browser's JIT engine. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does a compiler produce? - The program's output - Bytecode only + Machine code, before the program runs > C, C++, Rust and Go compile ahead of time into an executable. ? What is a virtual machine in the sense of the JVM? - A computer rented in the cloud + A program that runs bytecode - A faster kind of CPU > Bytecode is an instruction set for an imaginary computer; the JVM runs Java bytecode on whatever real computer it is on. ? Why can JavaScript be fast despite starting as source code? - Browsers have special JavaScript CPUs + Its engine compiles hot code while it runs - It is never interpreted at all > The engine JIT-compiles the parts that run often into machine code on the fly. ? When is an error in an interpreted language's code often found? - When the program is compiled + Only when that line actually runs - Never > There is no separate compile step to check everything first. ```

cards.a:
Machine code, before the program runs

C, C++, Rust and Go compile ahead of time into an executable.

cards.q: What is a virtual machine in the sense of the JVM?
cards.a:
A program that runs bytecode

Bytecode is an instruction set for an imaginary computer; the JVM runs Java bytecode on whatever real computer it is on.

cards.q: Why can JavaScript be fast despite starting as source code?
cards.a:
Its engine compiles hot code while it runs

The engine JIT-compiles the parts that run often into machine code on the fly.

cards.a:
